tldr: To overcome the limits of relying on static domain randomization (DR) in simulation, this paper proposes an approach that adapts a learned dynamics model using just 30 minutes of real-world data and then safely fine-tunes the policy inside it using on-policy RL (PPO). The method achieves stable bipedal walking even under harsh conditions far beyond prior assumptions, such as adding a 15 kg payload (around 80% of the robot's self-weight) or walking on an oil-lubricated ultra-low-friction surface.
hero_caption: Overall view of the proposed framework. (a) Pre-train the policy and dynamics model in simulation using a teacher-student setup, (b) collect real-world data using diverse behavioral policies, (c) adapt the dynamics model to the target environment with real-world data, and (d) further train the policy with PPO inside simulation using the adapted model as a surrogate environment.
overview:
When applying reinforcement learning to legged robot locomotion, domain randomization (DR)—randomly varying friction, mass, and other parameters in a simulator—is widely used to achieve robustness. However, if real-world variations exceed the range assumed during training, the robot either falls over or adopts an overly conservative gait, crouching deeply with bent knees to avoid falling under any circumstance.

To address this, the authors took a model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) approach: "Why not use a small amount of real-world data to fine-tune a dynamics model (a neural network predicting the environment's physical behavior) to the site, and then re-train the policy with on-policy RL (PPO) inside that learned model?" The key is decoupling real-world interaction, limiting it strictly to data collection while running policy optimization entirely inside a neural surrogate simulator. Furthermore, to prevent hallucination (predicting falsely stable trajectories) caused by model prediction errors, they introduced data collection with diverse behavioral policies and an uncertainty penalty via ensembling.

Evaluating the proposed method on "TRON 1," a point-foot bipedal robot weighing around 19 kg, showed striking results. When loaded with a 15 kg payload (around 80% of its self-weight) or walking on an extremely slippery oiled floor, conventional DR and prior adaptation methods (such as RMA and SysID) fell or broke down. In contrast, the proposed method walked stably and gracefully without losing its posture. This clearly demonstrates the effectiveness of a two-stage adaptation of the model and policy to field data, rather than blindly expanding the prior randomization range.
contributions: Proposed an adaptation framework that performs on-policy reinforcement learning inside a learned dynamics model adapted with real-world data, handling physical variations beyond static domain randomization ranges.

Designed a single-stage pre-training architecture that applies a teacher-student paradigm simultaneously to both the policy and the dynamics model, leveraging privileged information (contact forces and exact base velocities available only in simulation) for the teacher and purely proprioceptive information for the student.

Mitigated dynamics model hallucination (overly optimistic false predictions) that occurs when collecting real-world data with a single policy, greatly improving the model's predictive reliability by using an ensemble of diverse behavioral policies.

Demonstrated high adaptability and walking performance on a physical point-foot bipedal robot under extreme conditions, including an 80% self-weight (15 kg) payload and an oil-lubricated low-friction floor.

sections.heading: Why is conventional domain randomization alone not enough?
sections.summary: Domain randomization (DR), the standard way to bridge the sim-to-real gap, either collapses or becomes overly conservative when facing large out-of-distribution physical variations such as major payload increases or severe hardware degradation. This work proposes a framework that updates a learned dynamics model with a small amount of real-world data and re-trains the policy inside that model.
sections.details:
Reinforcement learning for legged robot control has achieved remarkable results, but much of that success relies on domain randomization (DR: randomly perturbing parameters like friction and mass during training) within physics simulators. However, pre-defined static parameter ranges have inherent limitations. When payload shifts or severe wear exceed what was anticipated, the learned policy either prioritizes stability by adopting an overly conservative crouch or, in the worst case, tips over.

System identification (SysID) aims to estimate physical parameters to address this, but it cannot fix structural discrepancies in the rigid-body dynamics model itself, such as nonlinear damping or actuator response delays. Local models like actuator nets also fail to capture system-wide variations.

To tackle this, the paper proposes learning a system-level dynamics model with a neural network and adapting it to the real-world environment. Using a small amount of offline trajectory data collected on the real robot, the dynamics model is aligned to the target environment. It is then used as a "surrogate simulator" to run on-policy training with PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization, a stable policy gradient algorithm).

The advantage of this method is the separation of real-world data collection from policy optimization. Thousands of rollout steps can be executed safely and swiftly on GPUs to polish the policy without requiring extra real-world interactions.

sections.heading: How does this differ from prior adaptation methods and world models?
sections.summary: Methods like RMA that infer environmental latent variables from history lack a forward causal predictive model, making them slow to react to extreme disturbances. Unlike conventional model-based RL (MBRL), this approach combines pre-trained model adaptation with privileged information distillation, enabling high-precision policy improvement from a modest amount of real-world data.
sections.details:
Environment adaptation methods for legged robots generally fall into several families.

### History-Based Adaptation
A leading example is RMA (Rapid Motor Adaptation), which compresses past proprioception history (such as joint angles) using an encoder to infer latent environmental parameters and feeds them to the policy. However, these methods merely learn correlations between history and privileged states (like friction coefficients or base velocity); they do not predict forward physical causality. As a result, when large unforeseen disturbances occur, latent variable estimation breaks down, leaving the robot with only reactive, makeshift responses.

### Learned Dynamics and MBRL
There are hybrid approaches combining rigid-body simulators with actuator or residual models, as well as methods that learn world models from offline data (such as Dreamer). However, latent-space models like Dreamer make interpretation and the injection of privileged simulator information difficult. In addition, learning policies from scratch purely on offline data presents data efficiency and stability challenges in robot control.

### Uniqueness of this Method
This work adopts a Transformer-based dynamics model that makes predictions over an explicit physical state space. Moreover, by applying the teacher-student paradigm concurrently to both the policy and the dynamics model, the model gains the ability to predict "privileged information" available only in simulation. When adapting with real-world data, only the proprioceptive prediction branch needs to be fine-tuned, achieving a clean separation.

sections.heading: From concurrent pre-training to model adaptation and PPO in a surrogate environment
sections.summary: The framework proceeds in four stages: concurrently pre-training the policy and a causal Transformer dynamics model in simulation, collecting real-world data using diverse policies, adapting the proprioceptive branch to real-world data, and fine-tuning with PPO using a reward that incorporates a model uncertainty penalty.
sections.details:
### III-A Problem Formulation and Error Decomposition
The dynamics error $\epsilon^{t}_{m}$ in the target environment can be decomposed via the triangle inequality into the sum of the simulator error during pre-training $\epsilon_{\text{pre}}$ and the shift error $\epsilon_{\text{shift}}$ capturing physical changes from the source to the target environment. The goal of this approach is to keep $\epsilon_{\text{pre}}$ low by capturing fundamental physical laws during pre-training, while minimizing $\epsilon_{\text{shift}}$ through model updates with real-world data.

### III-B Online Pre-training in Simulation
Four modules are trained concurrently in simulation in a single stage:
- **Teacher Policy and Student Policy**: While the teacher policy, which receives privileged information (base velocity, external forces, contact states, etc.), is trained with PPO, its features are distilled into the student policy, which takes only proprioceptive history (joint positions/velocities, IMU data) as input.
- **Two Branches of the Dynamics Model**: The proprioceptive branch predicting physical states and the privileged branch predicting privileged information needed for reward computation are trained in parallel.

### III-C Neural Dynamics Model Architecture
The backbone of the model is a GPT-2-style causal Transformer (6 layers, 12 heads). Taking past sequences of 16-step state-action tokens as input, it autoregressively predicts future states. In addition, a dynamics vector $z^d$ embedding simulation parameters $\xi$ is injected into each layer via FiLM (Feature-wise Linear Modulation), enabling behavior switching based on physical properties. The output layer features an ensemble MLP head, where the variance across heads yields the epistemic uncertainty (the model's own lack of confidence).

### III-D Real-World Offline Adaptation and RL in Surrogate Environment
For real-world data collection, instead of using a single converged policy, a "diverse behavioral policy set"—including intermediate pre-training checkpoints and injected noise—is deployed on the robot. This sufficiently excites the state-action space and prevents model "hallucination" (false optimistic predictions). Using the gathered real-world data, only the proprioceptive branch is fine-tuned with autoregressive loss, while the privileged branch remains frozen.

Once adaptation is complete, the student policy is further trained with PPO inside this dynamics model. An uncertainty penalty $\beta \sigma_e$ ($\beta < 0$) based on ensemble variance is subtracted from the reward, discouraging the policy from exploring unfamiliar regions where model predictions are uncertain.

sections.heading: An 80% payload overload and oiled floors: breaking through extreme conditions
sections.summary: Using the point-foot bipedal robot "TRON 1" (weighing around 19 kg), the method was evaluated under a 15 kg payload addition and an oil-lubricated floor. The proposed approach outperformed baseline methods (Narrow/Wide-DR, RMA, SysID) in both Sim-to-Sim and Sim-to-Real, recording an 80% walking success rate under payload overload and 100% on the oiled floor in hardware experiments.
sections.details:
### IV-A Experimental Setup
Evaluations were conducted on "TRON 1," a point-foot bipedal robot (approx. 19 kg self-weight) with a tiny support polygon that makes balancing exceptionally difficult. Two test conditions were used: (a) an ultra-high load condition carrying 15 kg (approx. 80% of self-weight) on the torso, and (b) an ultra-low-friction surface lubricated with oil (friction coefficient approx. 0.25). Baselines included Narrow-DR, Wide-DR, latent-adaptation RMA, and system-identification-based SysID. Real-world data was collected for about 30 minutes.

### IV-B Model Fidelity Analysis (Suppressing Hallucination)
Combining the Transformer backbone, autoregressive (AR) loss, and dynamics conditioning minimized accumulated error over long-horizon 100-step predictions. Furthermore, training on data from diverse behavioral policies ($N=320$) dramatically eliminated hallucination where the model falsely claimed the robot was "walking stably," boosting the policy's obtained reward from 0.15 to 0.90.

### IV-C Sim-to-Sim Transfer Results (MuJoCo Validation)
In transfer experiments from IsaacSim to MuJoCo, Narrow-DR could not withstand the 15 kg weight and fell backward immediately. Wide-DR did not fall, but it bent its knees to an extreme degree into a "crouch-walk," failing as a proper bipedal gait. While RMA and SysID maintained locomotion, they suffered from larger tracking errors and power consumption. The proposed method improved velocity tracking error by 45.4% and cut power consumption by 33.8% compared to RMA, also showing over 25% improvement against SysID.

### IV-D Ablation Studies
Removing dynamics conditioning reduced the success rate by 10–13 percentage points, confirming the critical role of the model's architectural design. For the uncertainty penalty coefficient $\beta$, setting it to zero ($\beta=0$) caused failures by rushing into uncertain areas, while making it too strict ($\beta=-10$) overly suppressed exploration and degraded performance; a moderate value ($\beta=-1$) proved optimal.

### IV-E Real-Robot Validations
In experiments on the physical "TRON 1," Narrow-DR suffered from severe torso sagging and erratic stepping, failing in all trials. In contrast, the policy adapted with the proposed method maintained an upright posture and rhythmic swing-stance cycles. Across five trials, it achieved an 80% success rate with the 15 kg payload and 100% on the oiled floor, and also succeeded in outdoor load-carrying walking.

sections.heading: Summary and future outlook
sections.summary: Rather than widening static domain randomization, this work established a new paradigm: completing on-policy reinforcement learning inside a world model adapted with real-world field data. Moving forward, investigating safer and automated mechanisms for real-world data collection will be an exciting frontier.
sections.details:
This paper demonstrated a novel framework that moves beyond static domain randomization by re-training policies on-policy inside a neural dynamics model adapted using real-world data. Conventional methods that widen simulation randomization ranges in pursuit of robustness often lead to overly conservative behavior or failure under extreme environmental shifts. In contrast, this approach enables efficient and aggressive adaptation tailored to the target environment.

Validations on a physical point-foot bipedal robot confirmed that even under extreme conditions—such as a payload reaching 80% of self-weight or an oil-coated low-friction floor—the robot successfully adapted its locomotion after just 30 minutes of prior data collection.

The authors highlight safety during real-world data collection as a future challenge. When encountering unfamiliar environments in the field, figuring out how to safely acquire excitation signals (diverse behavioral data) useful for dynamics identification while minimizing the risk of robot falls or damage remains an important research topic toward practical deployment.

takeaways: Widening DR too much forces the robot into an overly conservative, inefficient crouch; thus, "moderately narrow DR + world model adaptation via field data" is an effective solution.
Even when real-world data is limited in model-based RL, using "data collected from diverse policies" strongly prevents the model from hallucinating falsely stable trajectories.

Teacher-student distillation is highly effective not just for policies but also for dynamics models; separating branches for privileged information (for rewards) and proprioceptive information (for state transitions) is a practical key.
Incorporating uncertainty derived from an ensemble model as a reward penalty prevents the policy from overfitting (exploiting) dangerous regions where model predictions are inaccurate.
limitations: Requires roughly 30 minutes of data collection in the target real-world environment for adaptation, meaning it is not a purely zero-shot (instant, pre-interaction) adaptation method.

Deploying diverse behavioral policies during real-world data collection carries an inherent potential risk of the robot falling or sustaining damage during the data collection phase in unfamiliar environments.

Real-world evaluations are limited to flat-ground locomotion (such as walking straight and turning) on a point-foot bipedal robot; generalizability to rough terrain traversal or whole-body coordination tasks with heavy manipulation remains unverified.
